title: The Strange Menstrual Detail Hidden Inside Rachel’s Escape From Laban
paragraphs: The Strange Menstrual Detail Hidden Inside Rachel’s Escape From Laban

She sat on her father’s stolen gods and said she was menstruating. It sounds like one of the strangest details in Genesis—until you realize the scene exposes something terrifying about the idols we hide, the lies we inherit, and the God who refuses to abandon broken families.
There is a sentence in Genesis that almost nobody puts on a coffee mug.
Nobody stitches it onto a decorative pillow.
Nobody chooses it as the inspirational verse beneath a sunrise.
Yet once you understand what is happening, you may never read Rachel’s story the same way again.
Her father is searching the tent.
Rachel knows exactly what he is looking for.
She knows exactly where it is.
Because she stole it.
And now she is sitting on it.
Genesis 31:34 tells us that Rachel had taken her father Laban’s teraphim—his household gods—hidden them inside the camel’s saddle equipment, and sat down over them.
Then her father entered.
Imagine the tension.
Laban has pursued Jacob and his household after their sudden departure. He believes something belonging to him has disappeared.
He searches.
Tent after tent.
Possession after possession.
Then he reaches Rachel.
And Rachel says something so strangely intimate that modern readers can easily hurry past it:
“Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me.”
That expression comes from the Hebrew:
כִּי־דֶרֶךְ נָשִׁים לִי
ki derekh nashim li
Literally, something close to:
“For the way of women is upon/with me.”

The key expression is דֶּרֶךְ נָשִׁים — derekh nashim, “the way of women,” a Hebrew euphemism referring here to menstruation. Modern translations therefore understandably render Rachel’s words more directly: she is saying that she is having her period. Genesis then delivers the almost darkly comic conclusion:
Laban searches.
And does not find the gods.
Read that again.
The gods are there.
Laban is looking for them.
Rachel is sitting over them.
And they cannot save themselves.
That is where this strange little story begins opening into something much larger.
But first, we need to be careful.
The Bible tells us that Rachel stole the teraphim. It does not explicitly tell us why.
That distinction matters.

Some interpreters have connected household gods in the ancient world with family authority, inheritance, divination, or domestic religion. Those possibilities can illuminate the background, but Scripture itself does not stop the narrative and say, “Rachel stole them because of this specific reason.”
We should never turn an interesting possibility into a biblical certainty.
What Scripture does make certain is strange enough.
Genesis 31:19 says Rachel stole her father’s teraphim.
The Hebrew word is:
הַתְּרָפִים — hatteraphim

The teraphim were household cult objects or idols. In Genesis 31:34, Rachel conceals them in the camel’s equipment and sits over them. When Laban arrives, she explains that she cannot rise because “the way of women” is upon her.
And there she sits.
A daughter running from her father.
A wife traveling with her husband.
A woman carrying something from the house she is leaving.
Hidden underneath her are the gods of her past.
That image should make us uncomfortable.
Because some of us have done exactly the same thing.
Not literally.
But spiritually.
We left the house...
and brought the idols with us.
You can leave a toxic environment without leaving everything that environment planted inside you.
You can escape someone’s manipulation while still thinking according to their manipulation.
You can walk away from an unhealthy family system and still carry its wounds into your marriage.
You can reject your parents’ sins and unconsciously repeat their patterns.
You can change churches, cities, relationships, careers, countries...
and still carry the old gods beneath the saddle.
Rachel physically left Laban.
But something belonging to Laban traveled with her.
And that should terrify anyone who has ever thought, “Once I get away from this situation, everything inside me will finally be okay.”
Sometimes freedom requires more than changing geography.
Sometimes Egypt leaves your address before Egypt leaves your heart.
Sometimes Babylon is no longer around you, but Babylon is still talking inside you.
Sometimes you have escaped the person who wounded you, yet their voice still determines your worth.
And sometimes the hardest idols to surrender are not statues.
They are identities.
Control.
Approval.
Money.
Romance.
Success.
Reputation.
Comfort.
Being needed.
Being admired.
Being right.
Even religious appearance.
Anything we ask to give us what only God can ultimately give us can begin occupying sacred territory in the heart.
And the frightening thing about an idol is that you can hide it while continuing your journey with God.
Rachel’s story is not presented as a sanitized portrait of spiritual perfection.
Neither is Jacob’s.
That matters.
Because Genesis is brutally honest about this family.
Jacob deceives.
Laban deceives.
Rachel deceives.
People manipulate one another.
People hide things.
People compete.
People wound each other.
And God continues moving His covenant purposes forward—not because human beings are morally impressive, but because God is faithful.
That does not mean God approves of their sin.
Grace is not divine applause for dysfunction.
Grace is God accomplishing His redemptive purposes among people who desperately need Him.
And that is where this ancient tent begins pointing beyond Rachel.
Beyond Jacob.
Beyond Laban.
Beyond stolen household gods.
Toward Jesus Christ.
But before we get there, notice the devastating irony inside Rachel’s hiding place.
Later, under the Mosaic law, menstruation would involve ritual uncleanness, including uncleanness associated with what a menstruating woman sat upon (Leviticus 15:19–23).

We must not carelessly read the later Sinai legislation backward and pretend Genesis explicitly says Laban was applying Leviticus centuries before Moses. Genesis does not tell us precisely what Laban thought.
But the literary image remains striking.
Rachel is sitting on the gods.
The objects Laban considers valuable enough to chase after cannot speak.
Cannot expose her.
Cannot climb out.
Cannot defend themselves.
Cannot announce their location.
Cannot rescue their owner.
They have to be searched for.
They have to be carried.
They have to be protected.
They have to be recovered.
What kind of god needs a human being to rescue it?
The Bible will later mock idolatry with precisely this kind of devastating logic.
Isaiah describes people using part of a tree for ordinary purposes and turning another part into an idol before which they bow (Isaiah 44:9–20).
Psalm 115 describes idols as having mouths that cannot speak, eyes that cannot see, ears that cannot hear, and feet that cannot walk.
The biblical contrast is relentless.
False gods have to be carried.
The true God carries His people.
False gods have to be protected.
The true God protects His people.
False gods depend upon worshipers for their existence.
The true God existed before worshipers existed.
False gods cannot find you.
The true God found Adam behind the trees.
Found Hagar in the wilderness.
Found Jacob in his wandering.
Found Moses in Midian.
Found Elijah exhausted beneath a tree.
Found Jonah running in the opposite direction.
Found Peter after denial.
Found Saul while Saul was persecuting Christians.
And if you belong to Christ, He found you too.
Maybe that is why this strange story hurts.
Because if we are courageous enough to stop laughing at Laban’s gods, we may notice our own.
What are you sitting on?
What have you hidden so carefully that everyone assumes it is gone?
What are you carrying from the house God brought you out of?
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your children do not know.
Your followers certainly do not know.
You learned Christian vocabulary.
You learned when to say “Amen.”
You learned what to post.
You learned which worship songs make you cry.
You learned how to look strong.
But underneath the carefully arranged life...
something is still hidden.
A private addiction.
An affair in the imagination.
Bitterness you secretly enjoy rehearsing.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Money that has become your security.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A hunger for attention disguised as ministry.
Unforgiveness disguised as discernment.
Pride disguised as standards.
Fear disguised as wisdom.
Control disguised as responsibility.
And maybe you have become very good at keeping everyone from looking underneath.
That is the dangerous part.
Rachel fooled Laban.
You may fool people too.
But you cannot fool God.
Hebrews 4:13 says that no creature is hidden from His sight.
Nothing.
Not the browser history.
Not the secret conversation.
Not the resentment.
Not the fantasy.
Not the jealousy.
Not the compromise.
Not the idol.
And strangely, that is not merely frightening.
For the person willing to repent, it is incredibly hopeful.
Because the God who sees what is hidden is also the God who came to save sinners.
Christianity does not announce that good people can improve themselves until God accepts them.
Christianity announces something far more scandalous.
God came for sinners.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose for sinners.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity needed motivational improvement.
He went because sin is deadly.
We did not need polishing.
We needed reconciliation.
We did not need another household god.
We needed a Savior.
And this is where Rachel’s strange story collides with the Gospel.
The gods beneath Rachel could not save themselves.
But the true God came to save us.
Jesus was not an idol carried helplessly by human hands.
He willingly carried a cross.
Jesus was not hiding from humanity.
He entered humanity.
Jesus was not powerless before death.
He entered death and rose victorious over it.
Jesus does not need you to protect His throne.
He calls you to surrender yours.
And maybe the deepest question in this story is not:
“Why did Rachel steal the idols?”
Maybe the question that follows us home is:
What am I still carrying that Jesus is asking me to surrender?
Because repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what is hidden.
Repentance turns.
It brings the hidden thing into the light.
It stops defending what Christ died to free us from.
Some of us want Jesus and the teraphim.
Jesus and our secret sin.
Jesus and our bitterness.
Jesus and our obsession with approval.
Jesus and our control.
Jesus and our private idol.
We want salvation without surrender.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
But Jesus did not come merely to decorate the old life.
He came to make us new.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).
Not improved camouflage.
New creation.
That does not mean Christians instantly become flawless.
Look at the disciples.
Look at Peter.
Look at the churches addressed in the New Testament.
Transformation can involve painful battles, repeated dependence, confession, discipline, growth, and sanctification.
But grace changes the direction of our allegiance.
We stop making peace with the idol.
We begin bringing it to Christ.
And perhaps somebody reading this is exhausted from hiding.
You have been sitting over something emotionally for years.
Keeping people away from that part of your heart.
Making excuses whenever anyone gets close.
Smiling.
Serving.
Posting Scripture.
Going to church.
Saying, “I’m fine.”
But underneath...
you know.
Jesus knows too.
And He is not calling you deeper into hiding.
He is calling you into light.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Notice the Gospel.
Not:
“If you successfully hide your sin, God will love you.”
Not:
“If you punish yourself long enough, God might forgive you.”
Not:
“If you become impressive enough, Christ will receive you.”
Confess.
Come into the light.
Trust Christ.
The cross has already declared how seriously God takes your sin.
And the cross has also declared how astonishingly far His mercy reaches.
This is scandal becoming grace.
Not because sin stops being scandalous.
But because Jesus enters the scandal and writes redemption where we expected only condemnation.
Maybe your family story is messy.
Jacob’s was.
Maybe your father wounded you.
Maybe your mother failed you.
Maybe your marriage has scars.
Maybe you made decisions you wish you could erase.
Maybe there are chapters of your life you desperately hope nobody ever reads.
Scripture is filled with people whose biographies would never survive modern Christian image management.
Abraham failed.
Jacob deceived.
Judah fell spectacularly.
David committed grievous sin.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul once persecuted the church.
The Bible does not airbrush its people because the hero of Scripture is ultimately not its people.
It is God.
And redemption does not mean pretending the scandal never happened.
It means the scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That is why there is hope for the person reading this with tears in their eyes.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Your father does not write your ending.
Your addiction does not write your ending.
Your divorce does not write your ending.
Your failure does not write your ending.
Your shame does not write your ending.
Your past does not sit on the throne.
Jesus Christ does.
But do not confuse that hope with permission to keep the idols.
Grace is not an invitation to hide more comfortably.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
The same Christ who forgives calls us to follow Him.
So perhaps today is the day you stop sitting on what needs to be surrendered.
Name it before God.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Where appropriate, seek the help of mature believers who will walk with you in truth rather than merely soothe you in secrecy.
Destroy access to what keeps dragging you backward.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Make restitution where biblical repentance requires making wrongs right.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
And when you fail, do not run back toward the idol as though the idol can save you.
Run toward Christ.
The household gods beneath Rachel could not speak.
Jesus speaks.
They could not see.
Jesus sees.
They could not walk.
Jesus walked among us.
They could not rescue themselves.
Jesus walked out of His tomb.
That is the difference.
And maybe you know somebody who desperately needs to hear this.
Not somebody you want to embarrass.
Somebody you love.
Send it privately to the believer who feels too ashamed to come home.
an idol cannot save you, but Jesus can.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details. You do not owe strangers your private story.

And if Christ has already been breaking chains in your life, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed person finally believes that restoration is possible.
You cannot purchase God’s approval. Christ purchased our redemption.

But generosity, sharing truth, supporting faithful ministry, and helping biblical resources reach more people can genuinely become ways we choose to glorify God when they flow freely from faith and love rather than pressure.
But whether you ever spend a cent or not, hear this clearly:
Come to Jesus.
Not to us.
Not to merchandise.
Not to a page.
Not to a personality.
Jesus.
Because Rachel’s hidden gods could not save anyone.
Neither can ours.
The money cannot forgive you.
The relationship cannot redeem you.
The applause cannot cleanse you.
The addiction cannot comfort you without eventually demanding more.
The image cannot heal you.
The secret cannot protect you forever.
Only Christ can save.
Only Christ can forgive.
Only Christ can take the scandalous wreckage of human sin and, through the cross and resurrection, begin writing something the broken person thought could never exist again:
Grace.
So stop running with the idol underneath you.
Stop protecting what cannot protect you.
Stop carrying what cannot carry you.
Bring it into the light.
Lay it before Christ.
And discover that the God you were afraid would destroy you when He saw the truth is the God who already knew the truth when He stretched out His hands on the cross.
You can hide an idol beneath you from another human being—but you never have to hide your broken heart from the Savior who was crucified to bring sinners home.
